# 6.7 Asset Allocation: Key file (for the AI tutor only)

Do not reveal anything here before the learner has answered.

## Lesson facts relevant to the questions

- The learner has studied portfolio variance (Lesson 0.3, "Probability: Expectation, Variance, Covariance and Portfolio Variance" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/0-3-probability/, Lesson 4.2, "Mean–Variance Portfolio Theory" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/4-2-markowitz/), capital allocation and risk aversion (Lesson 4.3, "The Capital Allocation Line and the Capital Market Line" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/4-3-capital-allocation/), the market portfolio (Lesson 4.3, "The Capital Allocation Line and the Capital Market Line" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/4-3-capital-allocation/, Lesson 4.4, "The Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM)" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/4-4-capm/), market efficiency and behavioral finance (Lesson 4.7, "The Efficient Market Hypothesis" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/4-7-market-efficiency/, Lesson 4.8, "Behavioral Finance" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/4-8-behavioral-finance/), capital market assumptions and CAPE (Lesson 4.11, "Capital Market Assumptions" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/4-11-capital-market-assumptions/), lifecycle allocation and target-date funds (Lesson 4.12, "Life-Cycle Asset Allocation Theory" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/4-12-lifecycle-allocation/), exchange-rate risk and hedging (Lesson 2.7, "The Open Economy" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/2-7-open-economy/), accounts and taxes (Lesson 6.5, "Accounts and Taxes (US)" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/6-5-accounts-taxes/) and the household balance sheet (Lesson 6.6, "The Household Balance Sheet and Insurance" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/6-6-household-balance-sheet/). Percentages in percentage points; variance in %².
- The lesson: strategic allocation is the long-term target mix, set by goals and horizon, the lower of risk capacity (financial) and tolerance (psychological), and capital market assumptions; it goes into the IPS and does not change with short-term moves. Tactical allocation is a temporary departure on a short-term view, in effect market timing, facing the evidence on efficiency and costs.
- The lesson: glide paths, for example about 90% stocks 40 years before retirement and 40%–50% at retirement; "to" versus "through"; people with stable incomes or pensions can hold more stocks, people whose income moves with the market fewer; falls around retirement matter most (Lesson 6.9, "Retirement Planning" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/6-9-retirement-planning/).
- The lesson: US stocks are more than 60% of the global market (MSCI ACWI, 2025); home bias; the theoretical market portfolio is global; correlations between markets have been fairly high since 2000, so short-term volatility reduction is limited and the benefit is mostly long-run, e.g. the Nikkei 225's December 1989 peak was not surpassed until February 2024; currency risk in stocks is usually unhedged, in bonds usually hedged; some target-date funds hold about 40% of stocks outside the US.
- The lesson: rebalancing sells overweight and buys underweight assets; calendar and band rules (such as ±5 percentage points); costs: trading and capital gains tax in taxable accounts; ways to reduce them: use contributions, dividends and interest to buy underweights, adjust in tax-deferred accounts, trade only on large drifts. Figure 4-1: one fixed simulated path (stocks mean 7%, volatility 17%; bonds 4%, 6%; independent), 40 years; never rebalanced, stocks end at about 80%, peaking at about 90%; slider band ±1 to ±10 percentage points (steps of 1, default 5); rebalances: 36 at ±1, 10 at ±5, 4 at ±10. The lesson does not discuss whether rebalancing raises returns (left to Exercises Question 1).

## Check question C1

A young couple says they could accept a 50% fall in their portfolio, but this money is needed in 3 years for a house down payment, and the amount must be there then. In setting the allocation of this money, the main basis should be:

- (A) Risk capacity: with a short horizon and an amount that must be there, they cannot afford a large loss financially, so it should be mainly low-risk assets ← Correct answer
- (B) Risk tolerance: they can accept a 50% fall, so it can be mainly stocks
  Why it is wrong (tell the learner when they choose this option): When tolerance and capacity differ, which governs? If stocks are down 30% in 3 years, what happens to the down payment?
- (C) Capital market assumptions: stocks have higher long-run expected returns, so hold more stocks
  Why it is wrong (tell the learner when they choose this option): How much does long-run expected return matter for money that must be there in 3 years? How much do stock returns swing over that span?

**Reference answer**

(A). The strategic allocation follows the lower of risk capacity and tolerance. They can bear large swings psychologically, but this money has a short horizon and a fixed use; a fall of 30% or more within 3 years is not rare, and then they could not buy as planned. So this money's risk capacity is low, and it belongs mainly in short-term bonds or deposits; their high tolerance can show in their long-term retirement savings.

## Check question C2

Two 40-year-old investors have the same financial assets and the same risk aversion: one is a tenured professor with a pension, the other an investment banker whose income comes mainly from year-end bonuses and company stock. Following lifecycle allocation, whose financial assets suit a higher stock share?

- (A) The professor, because his human capital is stable and bond-like, so his financial assets can bear more stock risk ← Correct answer
- (B) The banker, because he understands financial markets
  Why it is wrong (tell the learner when they choose this option): Does understanding markets lower his risk? What happens to his income when stocks fall?
- (C) The same, since their age, wealth and risk aversion are the same
  Why it is wrong (tell the learner when they choose this option): Total wealth includes human capital. Is the risk of their human capital the same?

**Reference answer**

(A). The risk of total wealth depends on both human capital and financial assets (Lesson 4.12, "Life-Cycle Asset Allocation Theory" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/4-12-lifecycle-allocation/). The professor's income hardly moves with the market, so his human capital is like a large bond holding and his financial assets can hold more stocks; the banker's bonus, job and company stock all move closely with the market, so his human capital is stock-like and his financial assets should be more conservative, with fewer holdings tied to his employer and the financial industry.

## Check question C3

A US investor holds only an S&P 500 index fund. Since these large companies do business worldwide and earn much of their revenue abroad, he is already internationally diversified and needs no stocks outside the US.

Correct answer: False

Hint (give it after a wrong answer, without the verdict): Is earning revenue abroad the same as returns coming from a market? If valuations across the US market fell, what would happen to these companies' share prices?

**Reference answer**

False. Foreign revenue does give some exposure to foreign economies, but these stocks are all listed in the US, and their prices are driven together by US market valuations, interest rates and investor sentiment; they are highly correlated and cover only large US companies, not foreign or small companies. A country's market can slump for a long time because of high valuations or domestic problems, as Japan's did after 1989. Holding the global market diversifies that single-country risk.

## Check question C4

In Figure 4-1, narrow the rebalancing band from ±5 to ±1 percentage point. Which statement is correct?

- (A) The stock weight stays closer to 60%, but rebalancing happens far more often, adding trading costs and taxes ← Correct answer
- (B) The narrower the band the better, since risk is controlled more precisely at no extra cost
  Why it is wrong (tell the learner when they choose this option): Look at the number of rebalances in the readout. What does each rebalance mean in a taxable account?
- (C) The width of the band does not affect how often rebalancing happens
  Why it is wrong (tell the learner when they choose this option): Look at the readout: how many rebalances are there at ±5 and at ±1?

**Reference answer**

(A). On this path there are about 10 rebalances in 40 years at ±5 and about 36 at ±1, trading almost every year. A drift of 1 percentage point barely changes portfolio risk, yet the trading costs more and, in taxable accounts, realizes capital gains more often. The point of a band rule is to trade only when the drift matters for risk; about ±5 percentage points is a common compromise.

## Check question C5

A household's stock weight has drifted from its 60% target to 66%. Most of its stocks are in a taxable account with large unrealized gains; its 401(k) holds both stocks and bonds and receives new money every month. The most tax-efficient way to rebalance is:

- (A) Sell stocks and buy bonds inside the 401(k), and direct new contributions to bonds ← Correct answer
- (B) Sell stocks in the taxable account, since that is where most stocks are
  Why it is wrong (tell the learner when they choose this option): What does selling stocks with large gains in a taxable account cost? Is trading inside a 401(k) taxed?
- (C) No need to rebalance, since rebalancing always creates tax
  Why it is wrong (tell the learner when they choose this option): Does trading inside a 401(k) create tax? What about using new contributions to buy the underweight asset?

**Reference answer**

(A). Trades inside the 401(k) are not taxed, and new contributions can go straight to the underweight asset, so there is no need to sell appreciated stocks in the taxable account. Rebalancing looks at the mix across all accounts together, not each account by itself. Only if tax-deferred accounts and new money are not enough should selling in the taxable account be considered, choosing lots with small gains or losses first.

## Exercises Question 1 (id: Q1)

A 500,000 dollar portfolio starts the year at 60% stocks and 40% bonds. Over the year stocks rise 30% and bonds fall 5%.
(a) What is the stock weight at year end? How many stocks must be sold to return to 60/40 (thousand dollars)?
(b) A friend says: "Rebalancing sells winners and buys losers, and stocks have momentum (Lesson 4.6, "Multifactor Models" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/4-6-multifactor-models/), so rebalancing lowers returns and should be avoided." Evaluate this statement. Consider a simplified example: one asset first rises 50% and then falls by a third (back to its starting price), and the other is cash earning 0; compare holding 50/50 rebalanced each period with starting at 50/50 and never adjusting, and find each one's growth after two periods. What does the example show? In what kind of market does rebalancing earn less?

**Reference answer**

(a) Stocks $0.6 \times 1.3 = 0.78$, bonds $0.4 \times 0.95 = 0.38$, total 1.16; stocks are $\frac{0.78}{1.16} \approx 67.24\%$. Target stocks $0.6 \times 1.16 = 0.696$, so sell $0.78 - 0.696 = 0.084$, times 500, about 42 (thousand dollars), and buy bonds with it.
(b) The statement is wrong, or at least incomplete. Rebalancing is mainly about controlling risk: without it, the stock share keeps rising as stocks rise (to about 90% at one point in Figure 4-1), and the portfolio's risk is no longer the one chosen in the IPS. Whether it helps returns depends on how markets move. In the example, the unadjusted portfolio ends where it started, growth 0; the rebalanced one is $0.5 \times 1.5 + 0.5 = 1.25$ after the first period and $0.5 \times \frac{2}{3} + 0.5 \approx 0.833$ in the second, so $1.25 \times 0.833 \approx 1.0417$ after two, growth about 4.17%. In markets that swing back and forth, rebalancing sells high and buys low and gains. Conversely, in a market that keeps rising in one direction (stocks beating bonds for many years in a row), rebalancing keeps selling the rising asset and earns less than not rebalancing; momentum exists at horizons up to a year, while at the horizons of yearly or band rebalancing long-run reversal also exists (Lesson 4.7, "The Efficient Market Hypothesis" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/4-7-market-efficiency/). So rebalancing does not guarantee higher returns; what it buys is keeping risk at the chosen level.

**Grading points**

- (a) OK: about 67.24%, sell about 42 (thousand dollars).
- (b) OK: says rebalancing is mainly about controlling risk; computes about 4.17% growth with rebalancing and 0 without in the example, and explains that rebalancing earns less in trending markets. Only saying rebalancing is always better, or agreeing with the friend, needs revision.

Numeric answers: w = 67.24, sell = 42, bonus = 4.17

**Common errors**

- Thinking rebalancing "sells winners and buys losers" against momentum and so should be avoided; or thinking it always raises returns. Ignoring that its main purpose is controlling risk, and that it may gain in choppy markets and lose out in trending ones.

## Exercises Question 2 (id: Q2)

US stocks have a volatility of 16%, developed markets outside the US 18%, and their correlation is 0.8.
(a) What is the volatility of a stock portfolio of 60% US and 40% international? How much lower than 100% US?
(b) An investor concludes: "International stocks hardly reduce risk and are more volatile, so there is no point in holding them." Evaluate this statement.

**Reference answer**

(a) Variance $0.6^2 \times 16^2 + 0.4^2 \times 18^2 + 2 \times 0.6 \times 0.4 \times 0.8 \times 16 \times 18 = 92.16 + 51.84 + 110.59 = 254.59$ (%²), volatility about 15.96%, only about 0.04 percentage points below 16%.
(b) The arithmetic is right: with a correlation of 0.8 yearly volatility barely changes. But the conclusion does not follow. First, yearly volatility measures short-term risk, while the value of international diversification lies in avoiding a long slump in one country: Japan's market did not regain its 1989 high for over thirty years, and US stocks had a very low total return over the 2000s. This risk does not show in yearly correlations. Second, countries differ in valuations, sector mix and currency, so long-run returns can differ greatly, and no one knows in advance which country will do better. Third, in theory the market portfolio is global, and holding one country is a bet that it will win (Lesson 4.3, "The Capital Allocation Line and the Capital Market Line" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/4-3-capital-allocation/). Fourth, international stocks reduce volatility little but hardly add any; with similar expected returns, insurance against single-country risk at almost no cost is worth having.

**Grading points**

- (a) OK: about 15.96%, only about 0.04 percentage points lower.
- (b) OK: says yearly volatility hides the risk of a long single-country slump, with an example (Japan or another); mentions the global market portfolio or that no one knows which country will do better. Agreeing there is no point needs revision.

Numeric answers: sd = 15.96

**Common errors**

- Concluding that international diversification is useless because markets are highly correlated and adding foreign stocks cuts volatility little; ignoring the risk of a long single-country slump and the meaning of the global market portfolio.

## Exercises Question 3 (id: Q3)

An investor's strategic allocation is 60% stocks and 40% bonds. CAPE is now high, and using the building-block method (Lesson 4.11, "Capital Market Assumptions" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/4-11-capital-market-assumptions/) he estimates stocks will return only 5% a year over the next 10 years, and bonds 4%.
(a) By this estimate, what are the expected returns of 60/40 and 30/70?
(b) He plans to "cut stocks to 30% until valuations come down, then add them back". Evaluate this plan. If his estimate of stocks' expected return really has fallen, what would a reasonable adjustment look like?

**Reference answer**

(a) 60/40: $0.6 \times 5\% + 0.4 \times 4\% = 4.6\%$; 30/70: $0.3 \times 5\% + 0.7 \times 4\% = 4.3\%$.
(b) The plan is tactical timing with many problems. First, CAPE has some power to explain the next 10 years' returns but almost none for 1–2 years, and valuations can stay high for many years (Lesson 4.11, "Capital Market Assumptions" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/4-11-capital-market-assumptions/); "adding back after they come down" needs the timing right twice, and what counts as "down" is not defined in advance. Second, even by his own estimate stocks still earn more than bonds; the equity premium has shrunk, not vanished. Third, by capital allocation reasoning (Lesson 4.3, "The Capital Allocation Line and the Capital Market Line" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/4-3-capital-allocation/), the optimal stock share is proportional to the risk premium: if he used to expect stocks to beat bonds by 3 percentage points and now by only 1, scaling down is one line of thought, but premium estimates are very imprecise (Lesson 4.10, "Estimation Error and Robust Optimization" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/4-10-estimation-error/), and cutting from 60% to 30% at once leans too hard on one uncertain point estimate. A reasonable approach: write the lowered capital market assumptions into the IPS, adjust modestly within the ranges the strategic allocation allows (a few percentage points, say), and accept lower expected returns (save more or adjust goals), rather than going all in or all out.

**Grading points**

- (a) OK: 4.6% and 4.3%.
- (b) OK: says valuations predict poorly in the short run and timing must be right twice; by his own estimate stocks still carry a premium; recommends a modest adjustment based on capital market assumptions rather than all in or out. Agreeing with the plan needs revision.

Numeric answers: e60 = 4.6, e30 = 4.3

**Common errors**

- Timing the market all-in or all-out on a valuation measure, changing the stock share drastically; ignoring that valuations predict short-term returns poorly, and that even with lower expected returns, the allocation change implied by expected return and risk should be modest.

## Exercises Question 4 (id: Q4)

A household's portfolio is 1 million dollars with a 60% stock target. Stocks are now 70%, so about 100,000 dollars of stocks must be sold. In their taxable account the stocks' cost basis is only half their market value; the long-term capital gains rate is 15%. Their 401(k) holds 200,000 dollars, all in stocks.
(a) If they sell 100,000 dollars of stocks in the taxable account, how much tax is due (thousand dollars)?
(b) A friend says: "A rule is a rule; every year every account must be put back to 60/40." Evaluate this statement and give a better rebalancing plan.

**Reference answer**

(a) The gain is $100 \times 50\% = 50$, so the tax is $50 \times 15\% = 7.5$ (thousand dollars).
(b) The statement is wrong. Rebalancing targets the mix of the household's whole portfolio, not each account separately. A better plan: sell 100,000 dollars of stocks inside the 401(k) and buy bonds, with no tax at all, bringing the total stock share from 70% to 60%; afterwards direct new contributions and taxable dividends to the underweight asset first. This also fits asset location: bonds in the tax-deferred account, stocks in the taxable one (Lesson 6.5, "Accounts and Taxes (US)" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/6-5-accounts-taxes/). If selling in the taxable account cannot be avoided, sell lots with higher basis or losses first, and consider combining with tax-loss harvesting. Also, trading only when the drift exceeds a band avoids unnecessary trades.

**Grading points**

- (a) OK: 7.5 (thousand dollars).
- (b) OK: says rebalancing targets the overall mix; proposes tax-free ways such as trading in the 401(k) and using new money; mentioning asset location, lot selection or band rules is a plus. Agreeing with the friend needs revision.

Numeric answers: tax = 7.5

**Common errors**

- Thinking the portfolio must be returned exactly to target each time in whatever account; ignoring the tax cost of selling appreciated assets in taxable accounts, and that new money or tax-deferred accounts can do the rebalancing.
